metadata.title: A second-order gradient-like dissipative dynamical system with Hessian-driven damping. Application to optimization and mechanics

items.name: Assumption (H)
items.statement:
Throughout this paper, $H$ is a real Hilbert space with scalar product and norm denoted by $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ , respectively. Let $\Phi:H\to\mathbb{R}$ be a mapping satisfying:

$$
\begin{array}{l l} (\mathcal {H}) & \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \varPhi \text {is bounded from below on} H, \\ \varPhi \text {is twice continuously differentiable on} H, \\ \text {the Hessian} \nabla^ {2} \varPhi \text {is Lipschitz continuous on the bounded subsets of} H. \end{array} \right. \end{array}
$$
items.remark: [Note: local Hessian Lipschitzness is used to make the DIN phase vector field locally Lipschitz]

items.name: (DIN)
items.statement:
Given two parameters $\alpha > 0$ and $\beta > 0$ , consider the following second-order in time system in H:

$$
(\mathrm{DIN}) \quad \ddot {x} + \alpha \dot {x} + \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x) \dot {x} + \nabla \varPhi (x) = 0.
$$
items.remark: [Notation: formulate as a second-order ODE on the Hilbert space]

items.name: Strong monotonicity on bounded subsets
items.statement:
In this section we assume that $\Phi$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}^{2}(H)$ , with a Hessian Lipschitz continuous on bounded subsets, and that $\Phi$ is coercive with $\nabla\Phi$ strongly monotone on bounded subsets of H. More precisely, it is required that $\forall R > 0, \exists\beta_{R} > 0$ such that $\forall x, y \in H$ ,

$$
\max \left\{| x |, | y | \right\} <   R \quad \Rightarrow \quad \left\langle \nabla \Phi (x) - \nabla \Phi (y), x - y \right\rangle \geqslant \beta_ {R} | x - y | ^ {2}. \tag {5}
$$
items.remark: [Foundation: Operator.Linear] recall IsStronglyMonotone | [Notation: this is a local-in-radius variant]

items.name: Opial's Lemma
items.statement:
Lemma 5.1 (Opial). Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $x:[0, +\infty [\mapsto H$ a function such that there exists a nonempty set $S \subseteq H$ verifying:

(a) if $x(t_n) \rightharpoonup \bar{x}$ weakly in $H$ for some $t_n \to +\infty$ then $\bar{x} \in S$ ;  
(b) $\forall z\in S,\lim_{t\to +\infty}|x(t) - z|$ exists.

Then, $x(t)$ weakly converges as $t \to +\infty$ to an element of $S$ .
items.proof: Cited from: Z. Opial, Weak convergence of the sequence of successive approximations for nonexpansive mappings, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 73 (1967) 591–597.
items.source: Z. Opial, Weak convergence of the sequence of successive approximations for nonexpansive mappings, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 73 (1967) 591–597.
items.remark: [Foundation: Hilbert.WeakConvergence] recall opial_lemma

items.name: (g-DIN)
items.statement:
It is natural now to introduce the following first-order system (where g stands for generalized)

$$
(\mathrm{g} \text {-DIN}) \quad \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {x} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x) + a x + b y = 0, \\ \dot {y} + a x + b y = 0, \end{array} \right.
$$

which is a slight generalization of (18); indeed (g-DIN) is (18) if we set:

$$
a = \alpha - \frac {1}{\beta}, \quad b = \frac {1}{\beta}. \tag {19}
$$
items.remark: [Prove hint: set $a=\alpha-1/\beta$, $b=1/\beta$ to recover DIN]

items.name: Unconstrained and constrained minimizers
items.statement: For $\\Phi:H\\to\\mathbb{R}$ and $C\\subseteq H$, define $$\\operatorname{Argmin}\\Phi:=\\{z\\in H:\\forall y\\in H,\\ \\Phi(z)\\leq\\Phi(y)\\},\\qquad \\operatorname{Argmin}_{C}\\Phi:=\\{z\\in C:\\forall y\\in C,\\ \\Phi(z)\\leq\\Phi(y)\\}.$$ A point $a$ is called a critical point of a differentiable $\\Phi$ when $\\nabla\\Phi(a)=0$
items.remark: [Prove hint: unfold Argmin; for convex differentiable $Phi$, use the first-order convexity inequality]

items.name: $omega$-limit set of a trajectory
items.statement: For a trajectory $x:[0,\\infty[\\to H$, its $\\omega$-limit set is $$\\omega(x):=\\{a\\in H:\\exists t_n\\to\\infty\\text{ with }x(t_n)\\to a\\}.$$ The distance to a nonempty set $A$ is $\\operatorname{dist}(u,A):=\\inf_{a\\in A}|u-a|$.
items.remark: [Prove hint: in finite dimension, boundedness gives precompactness of the orbit]

items.name: Metric projection onto a closed convex set
items.statement: If $C\\subseteq H$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, then $P_C:H\\to C$ denotes the unique metric projection: $$P_Cu\\in C\\quad\\text{and}\\quad |u-P_Cu|=\\inf_{v\\in C}|u-v|.$$ It is characterized by $$\\langle v-P_Cu,\\,u-P_Cu\\rangle\\leq0\\qquad( v\\in C).$$
items.remark: [Foundation: Projection.BestApproximation] recall isChebyshev_of_nonempty_isClosed_convex | [Foundation: Projection.BestApproximation] recall eq_projectionPoint_iff_mem_and_inner_sub_right_nonpos_of_nonempty_isClosed_convex

items.name: Cauchy--Lipschitz continuation theorem
items.statement: Let $X$ be a Banach space and $F:X\\to X$ be locally Lipschitz. For every $Y_0\\in X$, the equation $\\dot Y=F(Y)$ has a unique maximal classical solution. If its maximal time $T_{\\max}$ is finite and $Y(t)$ has a finite limit as $t\\uparrow T_{\\max}$, then the solution extends past $T_{\\max}$.
items.proof: Cited from: standard Cauchy--Lipschitz/Picard--Lindel"of theorem for Banach-space ODEs.
items.remark: [Prove hint: show the phase-space vector field is locally Lipschitz, then use the continuation clause]

items.name: Bruck strong-convergence theorem for even convex gradient flows
items.statement: If $\\mathcal E$ is an even convex differentiable functional on a Hilbert space with nonempty minimizer set, then the trajectory of its gradient flow $\\dot X+\\nabla\\mathcal E(X)=0$ converges strongly to a minimizer under the hypotheses used in Proposition 5.2.
items.proof: Cited from: R. E. Bruck, Asymptotic convergence of nonlinear contraction semigroups in Hilbert space, J. Funct. Anal. 18 (1975), 15--26.
items.source: R. E. Bruck, Asymptotic convergence of nonlinear contraction semigroups in Hilbert space, J. Funct. Anal. 18 (1975), 15--26.
items.remark: [Note: apply after Proposition 6.1 to the even convex energy on $H	imes H$]

items.name: Energy $E_\lambda$
items.statement:
Along every trajectory of (DIN) and for $\lambda > 0$ define:

$$
E _ {\lambda} (t) = \lambda \Phi (x (t)) + \frac {1}{2} | \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \Phi (x (t)) | ^ {2}. \tag {1}
$$

In particular, we will write for short

$$
E (t) = E _ {\alpha \beta + 1} (t) = (\alpha \beta + 1) \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) + \frac {1}{2} \big | \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {2}. \tag {2}
$$
items.remark: [Prove hint: differentiate using the chain rule and substitute (DIN)]

items.name: $(\varepsilon\text{-DIN})$
items.statement:
For simplicity, take $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 1$ and, for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , consider a solution $x_{\varepsilon} \in C^{2}([0, \infty[;H)$ to the initial value problem ( $x_{\varepsilon}$ does exist, see [12]),

$$
(\varepsilon \text {-DIN}) \quad \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \varepsilon \ddot {x} _ {\varepsilon} + \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x _ {\varepsilon}) \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} + \nabla \varPhi (x _ {\varepsilon}) = 0, \quad t > 0, \\ x _ {\varepsilon} (0) = x _ {0}, \quad \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (0) = \dot {x} _ {0}, \end{array} \right.
$$
items.remark: [Note: existence is cited in the paper; the proposition assumes a classical solution]

items.name: (CN)
items.statement:
where $x_{0}, \dot{x}_{0} \in H$ are given. We are interested in the asymptotic behaviour of $x_{\varepsilon}$ as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ . Observe that ( $\varepsilon$ -DIN) may be considered as a singular perturbation of the following evolution equation:

$$
\text {(CN)} \quad \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x) \dot {x} + \nabla \varPhi (x) = 0, \quad t > 0, \\ x (0) = x _ {0}. \end{array} \right.
$$

This is the Continuous Newton method for the minimization of $\Phi$ , which is a continuous version of the well-known Newton iteration:

$$
\nabla^ {2} \varPhi \big (x ^ {k} \big) \big (x ^ {k + 1} - x ^ {k} \big) + \nabla \varPhi \big (x ^ {k} \big) = 0.
$$

The unique solution $x \in C^2([0, \infty[;H)$ of (CN) satisfies:
items.remark: [Prove hint: rewrite as $\frac d{dt}\nabla\Phi(x)+\nabla\Phi(x)=0$]

items.name: Lojasiewicz Lemma
items.statement:
Lemma 4.1 (Lojasiewicz). Let $\Phi : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function which is supposed to be analytic in a neighbourhood of a critical point $a$ . Then, there exist $\sigma > 0$ and $\theta \in ]0, 1/2[$ such that $^2$

$$
| x - a | <   \sigma \quad \Rightarrow \quad \left| \Phi (x) - \Phi (a) \right| ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant \left| \nabla \Phi (x) \right|.
$$
items.proof: Cited from: S. Lojasiewicz, Ensembles semi-analytiques, IHES Notes (1965).
items.source: S. Lojasiewicz, Ensembles semi-analytiques, IHES Notes (1965).
items.remark: [Note: the paper needs the local gradient inequality near a critical point]

items.name: Theorem 6.1
items.statement: Theorem 6.1. Suppose $\Phi\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(H)$ , and let the constants $\alpha,\beta,a,b$ satisfy $\beta\neq0$ and (19). The systems (DIN) and (g-DIN) are equivalent in the sense that $x$ is a solution of (DIN) if and only if there exists $y\in\mathcal{C}^{2}([0,+\infty[,H)$ such that $(x,y)$ is a solution of (g-DIN).
items.proof:
$$
\dot {x} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x) + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{\beta}\right) x + \frac {1}{\beta} y = 0. \tag {15}
$$

Differentiate (15) to obtain:

$$
\beta \bigg [ \ddot {x} + \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x) \dot {x} + \bigg (\alpha - \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg) \dot {x} \bigg ] + \dot {y} = 0,
$$

which, in view of (DIN), yields

$$
\beta \left[ - \nabla \varPhi (x) - \frac {1}{\beta} \dot {x} \right] + \dot {y} = 0. \tag {16}
$$

Adding (15) and (16) gives: [The $\dot x$ and $\nabla\Phi(x)$ terms cancel exactly, leaving (17).]

$$
\left(\alpha - \frac {1}{\beta}\right) x + \dot {y} + \frac {1}{\beta} y = 0. \tag {17}
$$

Collecting (15) and (17) gives the first-order system:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {x} + \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{\beta}\right) x + \frac {1}{\beta} y = 0, \\ \dot {y} + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{\beta}\right) x + \frac {1}{\beta} y = 0. \end{array} \right. \tag {18}
$$

Conversely, let $(x, y)$ be a solution of (18). Combining the two lines of (18) yields $\dot{y} = \dot{x} + \beta \nabla \Phi(x)$ , while differentiating the first equation yields

$$
\ddot {x} + \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x) \dot {x} + \bigg (\alpha - \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg) \dot {x} + \frac {1}{\beta} \dot {y} = 0.
$$

Substituting the value of $\dot{y}$ in the above equation gives (DIN) again. Thus (DIN) is equivalent to (18).
items.remark: [Prove hint: differentiate the coordinate relation and eliminate $\dot y$]

items.name: Theorem 6.2
items.remark: [Prove hint: repeat the Lyapunov calculation for the first-order system]

items.name: Gradient system (21) and energy (22)
items.statement:
Suppose $\Phi \in \mathcal{C}^1 (H)$ and $a > 0$ , $b > 0$ in (g-DIN). Rescaling the variable $y$ by $y = \sqrt{a / b} z$ transforms (g-DIN) into the equivalent system:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {x} + \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + a x + \sqrt {a b} z = 0, \\ \dot {z} + \sqrt {a b} x + b z = 0. \end{array} \right. \tag {20}
$$

We note that (20) is exactly the gradient system

$$
\dot {X} + \nabla \mathcal {E} (X) = 0, \tag {21}
$$

where $X = (x, z)$ and $E : H \times H \mapsto R$ is defined by:

$$
\mathcal {E} (X) = \beta \varPhi (x) + \frac {1}{2} \big | \sqrt {a} x + \sqrt {b} z \big | ^ {2}.
$$

Suppose now that $\varPhi$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}^2 (H)$ and let us turn to (DIN) which we know is equivalent to (g-DIN) with $a = \alpha -1 / \beta$ , $b = 1 / \beta$ . If $\alpha$ , $\beta$ satisfy $\alpha \beta >1$ in addition to $\alpha >0$ , $\beta >0$ , then $a$ , $b$ satisfy $a > 0$ , $b > 0$ . As a consequence, (DIN) is equivalent to the gradient system (20); using the parameters $\alpha$ , $\beta$ the expression of $\mathcal{E}$ is

$$
\mathcal {E} (X) = \mathcal {E} (x, z) = \beta \varPhi (x) + \frac {1}{2 \beta} \big | \sqrt {\alpha \beta - 1} x + z \big | ^ {2}. \tag {22}
$$
items.remark: [Notation: the gradient flow is on the product Hilbert space $H\times H$]

items.name: Properties of the $omega$-limit set of a bounded finite-dimensional trajectory
items.statement: For a bounded trajectory of a continuous autonomous flow in $\\mathbb{R}^N$, $\\omega(x)$ is nonempty, compact, and connected, and $\\operatorname{dist}(x(t),\\omega(x))\\to0$. If along the trajectory the velocity and the gradient of a $C^1$ Lyapunov potential tend to $0$, then every point of $\\omega(x)$ is a critical point of that potential.
items.proof: Cited from: A. Haraux, Systèmes Dynamiques Dissipatifs et Applications, RMA 17, Masson, 1991, as cited in the proof of Theorem 4.1.
items.source: A. Haraux, Systèmes Dynamiques Dissipatifs et Applications, RMA 17, Masson, 1991.
items.remark: [Note: the stated compactness uses the finite-dimensional hypothesis $H=mathbb{R}^N$]

items.name: (c-DIN), (H-c), and constrained energy
items.statement:
We propose in the following theorem to combine (g-DIN) and (S1) to solve $(\mathcal{P})$ . More precisely, given real parameters $\beta$ , a and b such that $\beta > 0$ , $a \neq 0$ , b > 0 and $b + a > 0$ , we consider the first-order system in $H \times H$ :

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \text {(c - DIN)} & \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {x} (t) + x (t) - P _ {C} \big [ x (t) - \beta \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big) - a x (t) - b y (t) \big ] = 0, \\ \dot {y} (t) + a x (t) + b y (t) = 0, \end{array} \right. \end{array}
$$

with initial conditions

$$
x (0) = x _ {0} \in C, \quad y (0) = y _ {0} \in H. \tag {27}
$$

Of course, (c-DIN) reduces to (g-DIN) if C = H. The functional $\Phi$ is required to satisfy the following hypotheses:

$$
\text {(H - c)} \quad \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \Phi \text {is defined and continuously differentiable} \\ \quad \text {on an open neighbourhood of the closed convex set} C, \\ \Phi \text {is bounded from below on} C, \\ \text {the gradient} \nabla \Phi \text {is Lipschitz continuous} \\ \quad \text {on the bounded subsets of} C. \end{array} \right.
$$

If $(x, y)$ is a solution to (c-DIN) and for $\lambda > 0$ , let us define:

$$
E _ {\lambda} (t) = \lambda \Phi \big (x (t) \big) + \frac {1}{2} \big | a x (t) + b y (t) \big | ^ {2}. \tag {28}
$$
items.remark: [Foundation: Projection.BestApproximation] recall eq_projectionPoint_iff_mem_and_inner_sub_right_nonpos_of_nonempty_isClosed_convex

items.name: Theorem 2.1
items.statement:
Theorem 2.1. Let $\Phi$ satisfy (H). Then the following properties hold for (DIN), provided $\alpha > 0$ and $\beta > 0$ :

(i) For each $(x_0, \dot{x}_0) \in H \times H$ , there exists a unique global solution $x(t)$ of (DIN) satisfying the initial conditions $x(0) = x_0$ and $\dot{x}(0) = \dot{x}_0$ , with $x \in \mathcal{C}^2([0, +\infty[;H])$ .  
(ii) For every trajectory $x(t)$ of (DIN) and $\lambda \in [(1 - \sqrt{\alpha\beta})^2, (1 + \sqrt{\alpha\beta})^2]$ , the scalar function $E_{\lambda}$ defined by (1) is bounded from below and decreasing on $[0, +\infty[$ , hence, it converges as $t \to +\infty$ . Moreover,

- $\dot{x}$ and $\nabla\Phi(x)$ belong to $L^{2}(0,+\infty;H)$ ;  
- $\lim_{t\to +\infty}\Phi (x(t))$ exists;  
- $\lim_{t\to +\infty}(\dot{x}(t) + \beta \nabla \Phi x(t)) = 0.$

(iii) Assuming, moreover, that $x \in L^{\infty}(0, +\infty; H)$ , we have:

- $\dot{x},\ddot{x},\nabla \Phi (x)$ and $\nabla^2\Phi (x)$ are bounded on $[0, + \infty [;$  
- $\lim_{t\to +\infty}\nabla \Phi (x(t)) = \lim_{t\to +\infty}\dot{x} (t) = \lim_{t\to +\infty}\ddot{x} (t) = 0.$
items.proof:
Proof. (i) For any choice of initial conditions $(x_{0},\dot{x}_{0})\in H\times H$ , the existence and uniqueness of a classic local solution to (DIN) follow from the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem applied to the equivalent first-order in time system in the phase space $H\times H$ , $\dot{Y}=F(Y)$ , with

$
Y (t) = \binom{x (t)}{\dot {x} (t)}

[The map $F$ is locally Lipschitz on $H\times H$: on every bounded ball the Hessian is bounded and Lipschitz, so $(u,v)\mapsto\nabla^2\Phi(u)v$ is locally Lipschitz, while $\nabla\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz there. Thus the hypotheses of the Cauchy--Lipschitz theorem hold.] \quad \text {and} \quad F (u, v) = \binom{v}{- \alpha v - \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (u) v - \nabla \varPhi (u)}.
$$

Let $x$ denote the maximal solution defined on some interval $[0, T_{\max}[$ with $0 < T_{\max} \leqslant +\infty$ . The regularity assumptions on $\Phi$ imply that $x \in \mathcal{C}^2([0, T_{\max}[; H])$ . Suppose, contrary to our claim, that $T_{\max} < +\infty$ . Differentiating $E(t)$ (see (2)) and using (DIN), we successively obtain:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \dot {E} (t) = (\alpha \beta + 1) \bigl \langle \nabla \Phi (x (t)), \dot {x} (t) \bigr \rangle + \bigl \langle \ddot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla^ {2} \Phi (x (t)) \dot {x} (t), \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \bigr \rangle \\ = (\alpha \beta + 1) \bigl \langle \nabla \Phi (x (t)), \dot {x} (t) \bigr \rangle - \bigl \langle \alpha \dot {x} (t) + \nabla \Phi (x (t)), \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \bigr \rangle \\ = - \alpha \left| \dot {x} (t) \right| ^ {2} - \beta \left| \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \right| ^ {2}. \tag {3} \\ \end{array}
$$

Hence, $E(t)$ is a Liapounov function for the trajectory x. Further, for all $t \in [0, T_{\max}[$ ,

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\alpha \beta + 1) \varPhi (x (t)) + \frac {1}{2} | \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)) | ^ {2} + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {t} | \dot {x} (\tau) | ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau \\ + \beta \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left| \nabla \varPhi (x (\tau)) \right| ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau = E (0). \tag {4} \\ \end{array}
$

Since $\Phi$ is bounded from below

[Integrating (3) from $0$ to $t$ gives (4), because $E$ is $C^1$ along the classical solution.  Since the first two terms of (4) are bounded below, both nonnegative integral terms are uniformly bounded.] and $\alpha, \beta > 0$ , we obtain that $\dot{x}$ and $\nabla \Phi(x)$ belong to $L^2(0, T_{\max}; H)$ . Therefore, for all $0 \leqslant s \leqslant t < T_{\max}$ ,

$$
\left| x (t) - x (s) \right| \leqslant \int_ {s} ^ {t} \left| \dot {x} (\tau) \right| \mathrm{d} \tau \leqslant \sqrt {t - s} \sqrt {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \left| \dot {x} (\tau) \right| ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau} \leqslant \sqrt {t - s} \| \dot {x} \| _ {L ^ {2} (0, T _ {\max}; H)},
$$

which shows that $\lim_{t\to T_{\max}}x(t)$ exists. As a consequence, $x$ is bounded on $[0,T_{\max}]$ and so is $\nabla^2\Phi (x)$ in view of the Lipschitz continuity of $\nabla^{2}\Phi$ . Thus

$$
\ddot {x} = - \alpha \dot {x} - \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x) \dot {x} - \nabla \varPhi (x)
$$

belongs to $L^{2}(0, T_{\max}; H)$ , and we have for all $0 \leqslant s \leqslant t < T_{\max}$ :

$$
\left| \dot {x} (t) - \dot {x} (s) \right| \leqslant \int_ {s} ^ {t} \left| \ddot {x} (\tau) \right| \mathrm{d} \tau \leqslant \sqrt {t - s} \| \ddot {x} \| _ {L ^ {2} (0, T _ {\max}; H)},
$$

so that $\lim_{t\to T_{\max}}\dot{x}(t)$ exists. Applying the Cauchy–Lipschitz local existence theorem to (DIN) with initial data at $T_{\max}$ given by $(\lim_{t\to T_{\max}}x(t),\lim_{t\to T_{\max}}\dot{x}(t))$ , we can extend the maximal solution to an interval strictly larger than $[0,T_{\max}[$ , which contradicts the maximality of the solution. Consequently, $T_{\max}=+\infty$ .

(ii) The point here is to realize that there is a whole family of Liapounov functions for the trajectory x. Indeed, setting for short (recall (1))

$$
E _ {\pm} (t) = E _ {1 \pm \sqrt {\alpha \beta}} = \left(1 \pm \sqrt {\alpha \beta}\right) ^ {2} \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) + \frac {1}{2} \big | \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {2},
$$

we obtain:

$$
\dot {E} _ {\pm} (t) = - \left| \sqrt {\alpha} \dot {x} (t) \mp \sqrt {\beta} \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \right| ^ {2}.
$

Hence, $E_{+}$ and $E_{-}$ are two Liapounov functions for $x$ , as well as any convex combination of them.

[Indeed $E_\lambda$ depends affinely on $\lambda$; every $\lambda$ in the displayed interval is obtained as a convex combination of $(1-\sqrt{\alpha\beta})^2$ and $(1+\sqrt{\alpha\beta})^2$, while the quadratic term is common to both endpoint energies.] As a result, for any $\lambda$ in $[(1 - \sqrt{\alpha\beta})^2, (1 + \sqrt{\alpha\beta})^2]$ , $E_{\lambda}$ is decreasing on $[0, +\infty[$ , (e.g., $E = E_{\alpha\beta + 1} = (1/2)(E^{+} + E^{-})$ ). Further we have:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(1 \pm \sqrt {\alpha \beta}\right) ^ {2} \varPhi (x (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \big | \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)) \big | ^ {2} - E _ {\pm} (0) \\ = - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left| \sqrt {\alpha} \dot {x} (\tau) \mp \sqrt {\beta} \nabla \Phi (x (\tau)) \right| ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau . \\ \end{array}
$$

Since $\Phi$ is bounded from below, we obtain that both

$$
\left| \sqrt {\alpha} \dot {x} - \sqrt {\beta} \nabla \Phi (x) \right| \quad \text {and} \quad \left| \sqrt {\alpha} \dot {x} + \sqrt {\beta} \nabla \Phi (x) \right|
$$

belong to $L^2(0, +\infty)$ and hence $\dot{x}$ and $\nabla \Phi(x)$ are in $L^2(0, +\infty; H)$ . [More explicitly, the sum of the squares of these two functions is $2\alpha|\dot x|^2+2\beta|\nabla\Phi(x)|^2$, so finiteness of both integrals gives the asserted two $L^2$ bounds.] Now, since $E_+$ and $E_-$ are decreasing and bounded from below, $\lim_{t \to +\infty} E_+(t)$ and $\lim_{t \to +\infty} E_-(t)$ exist. Therefore, $\Phi(x(t)) = (1/(4\sqrt{\alpha\beta})) (E_+(t) - E_-(t))$ admits a limit as $t \to +\infty$ . As a consequence, $|\dot{x}(t) + \beta\nabla \Phi(x(t))|$ has a limit as $t \to +\infty$ , which is zero because $|\dot{x}(t) + \beta\nabla \Phi(x(t))| \in L^2(0, +\infty)$ .

(iii) We now assume that $x$ is in $L^{\infty}(0, +\infty; H)$ . Then, by (H), $\nabla^{2}\Phi(x)$ and $\nabla \Phi(x)$ are bounded on $[0, +\infty[$ ; and so are $\dot{x} = (\dot{x} + \beta \nabla \Phi(x)) - \beta \nabla \Phi(x)$ and $\ddot{x} = -\alpha \dot{x} - \beta \nabla^{2}\Phi(x)\dot{x} - \nabla \Phi(x)$ . Set $h(t) = (1/2)|\nabla \Phi(x(t))|^{2}$ and note that $h \in L^{1}(0, +\infty)$ and $\dot{h} = \langle \nabla^{2}\Phi(x)\dot{x}, \nabla \Phi(x) \rangle \in L^{\infty}(0, +\infty)$ ; then, by a standard argument, $\lim_{t \to +\infty} h(t) = 0$ . [For completeness, if $h$ did not tend to $0$, there would be $\varepsilon>0$ and times $t_n\to\infty$ with $h(t_n)\geq\varepsilon$.  The bound on $\dot h$ supplies disjoint intervals of a fixed positive length on which $h\geq\varepsilon/2$, contradicting $h\in L^1$.] Likewise, if we set $k(t) = (1/2)|\dot{x}(t)|^{2}$ then $\lim_{t \to +\infty} k(t) = 0$ . [The same argument applies because $k\in L^1$ by (ii) and $\dot k=\langle\ddot x,\dot x\rangle$ is bounded.] It follows that $\ddot{x}(t) \to 0$ as $t \to +\infty$ .

items.name: Proposition 3.1
items.statement: Proposition 3.1. There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that $\forall t \geqslant 0$ , $|x_{\varepsilon}(t) - x(t)| \leqslant C\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ . Therefore, $x_{\varepsilon} \to x$ uniformly on $[0, +\infty[$ .
items.proof:
Proof. Let us introduce the $\varepsilon$ -energy

$$
U _ {\varepsilon} (t) := \frac {\varepsilon}{2} \big | \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big | ^ {2} + \varPhi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big),
$$

which satisfies

$$
\dot {U} _ {\varepsilon} (t) = - \big \langle \nabla^ {2} \varPhi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big) \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t), \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big \rangle \leqslant 0.
$

Hence,

$

[The inequality uses that strong monotonicity of $\nabla\Phi$ implies monotonicity, and differentiability then gives $\langle\nabla^2\Phi(x_\varepsilon)\dot x_\varepsilon,\dot x_\varepsilon\rangle\geq0$.]
U _ {\varepsilon} (t) \leqslant U _ {\varepsilon} (0) = \frac {\varepsilon}{2} | \dot {x} _ {0} | ^ {2} + \varPhi (x _ {0}), \tag {7}
$$

and consequently

$$
\sup _ {0 <   \varepsilon \leqslant 1} \sup _ {t \geqslant 0} \varPhi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big) \leqslant \frac {1}{2} | \dot {x} _ {0} | ^ {2} + \varPhi (x _ {0}) =: \alpha .
$$

Since $\Phi$ is coercive, the sublevel set $\Gamma_{\alpha}(\Phi):=\{x\in H:\Phi(x)\leqslant\alpha\}$ is bounded and then $\sup_{0<\varepsilon\leqslant1}\sup_{t\geqslant0}|x_{\varepsilon}(t)|<R$ for a suitable constant $R>0$ . Similarly, we obtain that the solution $x(t)$ of (CN) satisfies $\{x(t):t\geqslant0\}\subset\Gamma_{\Phi(x_0)}(\Phi)\subset\Gamma_{\alpha}(\Phi)$ , so that we may assume that $\sup_{t\geqslant0}|x(t)|<R$ . By (5), we have

$$
\forall t > 0, \quad \left| x _ {\varepsilon} (t) - x (t) \right| \leqslant \frac {1}{\beta_ {R}} \Big | \nabla \Phi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big) - \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big) \Big |. \tag {8}
$

Notice that the differential equation

[To obtain (8), combine (5) with Cauchy--Schwarz: $\beta_R|x_\varepsilon-x|^2\leq\langle\nabla\Phi(x_\varepsilon)-\nabla\Phi(x),x_\varepsilon-x\rangle\leq|\nabla\Phi(x_\varepsilon)-\nabla\Phi(x)|\,|x_\varepsilon-x|$, and cancel unless the distance is zero.] in ( $\varepsilon$ -DIN) may be rewritten:

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \big [ \varepsilon \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t) + \nabla \varPhi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big) \big ] + \nabla \varPhi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big) = 0.
$$

Setting $\omega_{\varepsilon}(t):=\varepsilon\dot{x}_{\varepsilon}(t)+\nabla\Phi(x_{\varepsilon}(t))$ , we obtain the nonhomogeneous initial value problem:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {\omega} _ {\varepsilon} + \omega_ {\varepsilon} = \varepsilon \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t), \quad t > 0, \\ \omega_ {\varepsilon} (0) = \varepsilon \dot {x} _ {0} + \nabla \Phi (x _ {0}), \end{array} \right.
$$

whose solution is given by:

$$
\omega_ {\varepsilon} (t) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- t} \big (\varepsilon \dot {x} _ {0} + \nabla \varPhi (x _ {0}) \big) + \varepsilon \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {- (t - \tau)} \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (\tau)   \mathrm{d} \tau .
$$

Thus

$$
\nabla \varPhi \big (x _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- t} \big (\varepsilon \dot {x} _ {0} + \nabla \varPhi (x _ {0}) \big) - \varepsilon \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t) + \varepsilon \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {- (t - \tau)} \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (\tau)   \mathrm{d} \tau .
$$

By (6) together with (8), we have:

$$
\left| x _ {\varepsilon} (t) - x (t) \right| \leqslant \frac {1}{\beta_ {R}} \Bigg (\varepsilon | \dot {x} _ {0} | + \varepsilon \big | \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (t) \big | + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {- (t - \tau)} \varepsilon \big | \dot {x} _ {\varepsilon} (\tau) \big |   \mathrm{d} \tau \Bigg).
$$

On the other hand, from the energy estimate (7), it follows that $\sup_{0 < \varepsilon \leqslant 1} \sup_{t \geqslant 0} \varepsilon |\dot{x}_{\varepsilon}(t)| \leqslant \sqrt{2\varepsilon(\alpha - \inf \Phi)}$ . Consequently,

$ [The convolution term is bounded by $\sup_{s\geq0}\varepsilon|\dot x_\varepsilon(s)|$, since $\int_0^t e^{-(t-\tau)}d\tau\leq1$.]
\big | x _ {\varepsilon} (t) - x (t) \big | \leqslant \frac {1}{\beta_ {R}} \big (\varepsilon | \dot {x} _ {0} | + 2 \sqrt {2 \varepsilon (\alpha - \inf \varPhi)} \big) \leqslant \frac {\sqrt {\varepsilon}}{\beta_ {R}} \big (| \dot {x} _ {0} | + 2 \sqrt {2 (\alpha - \inf \varPhi)} \big),
$$

which completes the proof. □
items.remark: [Prove hint: energy bound gives a common sublevel ball; use strong monotonicity and variation of constants]

items.name: Corollary 4.1
items.statement:
Corollary 4.1. Let $\Phi : \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function which is supposed to be analytic in the open set $\Omega$ . Let $A$ be a nonempty subset of $\Omega$ such that $\nabla \Phi(a) = 0$ , for all $a$ in $A$ :

(1) if A is connected then $\Phi$ assumes a constant value on A, say $\Phi_{A}$ ;  
(2) if $A$ is connected and compact, then there exist $\sigma > 0$ and $\theta \in ]0, 1/2[$ such that

$$
\mathrm{dist} (x, A) <   \sigma \quad \Rightarrow \quad \left| \Phi (x) - \Phi_ {A} \right| ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant \left| \nabla \Phi (x) \right|.
$$
items.proof:
Proof. (1) Pick some $a$ in $A$ . After the lemma there exist $\sigma > 0$ and $\theta \in ]0, 1/2[$ such that

$$
| x - a | <   \sigma \quad \Rightarrow \quad \left| \Phi (x) - \Phi (a) \right| ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant \left| \nabla \Phi (x) \right|.
$$

Hence, if x belongs to $A \cap B(a, \sigma)$ where $B(a, \sigma)$ is the open ball with center a and radius $\sigma$ , then $|\Phi(x) - \Phi(a)| = 0$ . As a consequence, the set $\{x \in A / \Phi(x) = \Phi(a)\}$ is open in A; as it is obviously closed in A and nonvoid it is equal to A. [A subset that is simultaneously open and closed in the connected space $A$ is either empty or all of $A$; it contains $a$, so it is all of $A$.]

(2) Without restriction we may assume that $\varPhi$ vanishes on $A$ . [Replace $\Phi$ by $\Phi-\Phi_A$; this leaves its gradient and the desired inequality unchanged.] According to Lojasiewicz's lemma and owing to the compactness of $A$ , there exists a finite family $(a_i, \sigma_i, \theta_i)_{i \in \{1, ..., n\}}$ with $a_i \in A$ , $\sigma_i > 0$ , $\theta_i \in ]0, 1/2[$ such that

- the balls $B(a_{i},\sigma_{i})$ , build a finite open cover of $A$ ;

$$
- x \in \Omega , | x - a _ {i} | <   \sigma_ {i} \Rightarrow | \varPhi (x) | ^ {1 - \theta_ {i}} \leqslant | \nabla \varPhi (x) |.
$$

Resorting once more to the compactness of $A$ , and to the continuity of $\varPhi$ , we assert the existence of some $\sigma > 0$ such that

$$
\mathrm{dist} (x, A) <   \sigma \quad \Rightarrow \quad x \in \Omega , \quad x \in \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n} B (a _ {i}, \sigma_ {i}), \quad \left| \varPhi (x) \right| \leqslant 1.
$$

If we set $\theta = \min \theta_{i}$ [Because $|\Phi(x)|\leq1$ and $\theta\leq\theta_i$, one has $|\Phi(x)|^{1-\theta}\leq|\Phi(x)|^{1-\theta_i}$.] , then any $x$ complying with $\mathrm{dist}(x,A) < \sigma$ verifies $x\in \Omega$ and $x\in B(a_i,\sigma_i)$ for some $i\in \{1,\dots ,n\}$ ; hence, $|\varPhi (x)|^{1 - \theta}\leqslant |\varPhi (x)|^{1 - \theta_i}\leqslant |\nabla \varPhi (x)|$ .
items.remark: [Prove hint: connected clopen argument, then a finite compactness cover]

items.name: Theorem 6.3
items.statement: Theorem 6.3. In addition to the hypotheses of Theorem 6.2 assume that $\Phi$ is convex and that $\operatorname{Argmin} \Phi$ , the set of minimizers of $\Phi$ on $H$ , is nonempty. Then for any solution $(x, y)$ of (g-DIN), $x(t)$ weakly converges to a minimizer of $\Phi$ on $H$ as $t$ goes to infinity.

items.name: Proposition 6.1
items.statement: Proposition 6.1. Suppose $\Phi \in \mathcal{C}^2 (H)$ , $\alpha >0$ , $\beta >0$ and $\alpha \beta >1$ . The system (DIN) is equivalent to the gradient system (21) with $\mathcal{E}$ given by (22).
items.proof:
Suppose $\Phi \in \mathcal{C}^1 (H)$ and $a > 0$ , $b > 0$ in (g-DIN). Rescaling the variable $y$ by $y = \sqrt{a / b} z$ transforms (g-DIN) into the equivalent system:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {x} + \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + a x + \sqrt {a b} z = 0, \\ \dot {z} + \sqrt {a b} x + b z = 0. \end{array} \right. \tag {20}
$$

We note that (20) is exactly the gradient system [Indeed the two partial gradients of $\mathcal E(x,z)=\beta\Phi(x)+\frac12|\sqrt a x+\sqrt b z|^2$ are $\beta\nabla\Phi(x)+ax+\sqrt{ab}z$ and $\sqrt{ab}x+bz$.]

$$
\dot {X} + \nabla \mathcal {E} (X) = 0, \tag {21}
$$

where $X = (x, z)$ and $E : H \times H \mapsto R$ is defined by:

$$
\mathcal {E} (X) = \beta \varPhi (x) + \frac {1}{2} \big | \sqrt {a} x + \sqrt {b} z \big | ^ {2}.
$$

Suppose now that $\varPhi$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}^2 (H)$ and let us turn to (DIN) which we know is equivalent to (g-DIN) with $a = \alpha -1 / \beta$ , $b = 1 / \beta$ . If $\alpha$ , $\beta$ satisfy $\alpha \beta >1$ in addition to $\alpha >0$ , $\beta >0$ , then $a$ , $b$ satisfy $a > 0$ , $b > 0$ . As a consequence, (DIN) is equivalent to the gradient system (20); using the parameters $\alpha$ , $\beta$ the expression of $\mathcal{E}$ is

$$
\mathcal {E} (X) = \mathcal {E} (x, z) = \beta \varPhi (x) + \frac {1}{2 \beta} \big | \sqrt {\alpha \beta - 1} x + z \big | ^ {2}. \tag {22}
$$
items.remark: [Prove hint: compute the two product-space partial gradients explicitly]

items.name: Theorem 7.1
items.proof:
The proof essentially goes along the same lines as in Theorem 2.1. The nonlinearity caused by the projection $P_C$ is compensated by the characteristic inequality $\langle v - P_C u, u - P_C u \rangle \leqslant 0$ for all $(u, v)$ in $H \times C$ . The natural quantities upon which the calculations rely are $\dot{x}$ and $\dot{y}$ (rather than $\dot{x}$ and $\nabla \Phi(x)$ in the proof of Theorem 2.1). [The projection inequality is precisely the characterization in ext_def_3, and the local phase-space vector field is locally Lipschitz because both $P_C$ and $\nabla\Phi$ are Lipschitz on bounded sets.]

Proof of Theorem 7.1. (i) Since the projection $P_C$ is a Lipschitz continuous operator, the local existence and the uniqueness of a solution to (c-DIN) with initial conditions (27) follow from the Cauchy-Lipschitz theorem. Let $(x, y)$ denote the maximal solution defined on some interval $[0, T_{\max}]$ with $0 \leqslant T_{\max} \leqslant +\infty$ .

First let us show that $x$ is viable for $t \in [0, T_{\max}[$ . Define $p: [0, T_{\max}[ \mapsto C$ by $p(t) = P_C[x(t) - \beta \nabla \Phi(x(t)) - ax(t) - by(t)]$ and integrate the equation $\dot{x} + x = p$ on $[0, t] \subset [0, T_{\max}[$ :

$$
x (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {- (t - s)} p (s) \mathrm{d} s + \mathrm{e} ^ {- t} x _ {0}.
$$

Observe that $\xi(t) = \int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{-(t - s)} / (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t})p(s)\mathrm{d}s$ belongs to $C$ , as the weight function $s\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-(t - s)} / (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t})$ is positive and its integral over $[0,t]$ is 1. Now writing $x(t) = (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t})\xi (t) + \mathrm{e}^{-t}x_{0}$ shows that $x(t)$ belongs to $C$ . [This uses convexity of $C$: $\xi(t)\in C$ is a normalized positive average of points of $C$, and $x(t)$ is its convex combination with $x_0\in C$.]

Next, the viability of $x$ and the convexity of $C$ are used to derive the following inequality on $[0, T_{\max}[:$

$$
\left\langle x - P _ {C} \big (x - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} \big), x - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} - P _ {C} \big (x - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} \big) \right\rangle \leqslant 0,
$$

which, in view of (c-DIN), successively reduces to

$$
\left\langle - \dot {x}, - \dot {x} - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} \right\rangle \leqslant 0, \quad \beta \left\langle \dot {x}, \nabla \Phi (x) \right\rangle \leqslant - | \dot {x} | ^ {2} + \langle \dot {x}, \dot {y} \rangle . \tag {29}
$$

Further, in order to apply classical energy arguments, we show that $E_{\lambda}$ defined by (28) is decreasing along the trajectory $(x, y)$ , at least for some value of $\lambda$ . Indeed, we have (using the second equation in (c-DIN)):

$$
\dot {E} _ {\lambda} = \lambda \big \langle \dot {x}, \nabla \varPhi (x) \big \rangle - b | \dot {y} | ^ {2} - a \langle \dot {x}, \dot {y} \rangle .
$$

Taking (29) into account, we obtain:

$$
\dot {E} _ {\lambda} \leqslant - \frac {\lambda}{\beta} | \dot {x} | ^ {2} - b | \dot {y} | ^ {2} + \left(\frac {\lambda}{\beta} - a\right) \langle \dot {x}, \dot {y} \rangle . \tag {30}
$$

In particular, if we choose $\lambda = \beta(a + 2b)$ (this last quantity is positive), we have:

$$
\dot {E} _ {\beta (a + 2 b)} \leqslant - (a + b) | \dot {x} | ^ {2} - b | \dot {x} - \dot {y} | ^ {2}. \tag {31}
$$

Integrating this inequality over $[0, t] \subset [0, T_{\max}[$ , we obtain:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \beta (a + 2 b) \Phi (x (t)) + \frac {1}{2} | a x (t) + b y (t) | ^ {2} + (a + b) \int_ {0} ^ {t} | \dot {x} (\tau) | ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau + b \int_ {0} ^ {t} | \dot {x} (\tau) - \dot {y} (\tau) | ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau \\ \leqslant \beta (a + 2 b) \Phi (x _ {0}) + \frac {1}{2} | a x _ {0} + b y _ {0} | ^ {2}. \tag {32} \\ \end{array}
$$

Finally, to prove that $(x,y)$ is defined over $[0, +\infty[$ , we suppose that $T_{\max} < +\infty$ and argue by contradiction. Since $x$ is viable and $\Phi$ is bounded from below, (32) shows that $\dot{y} = -(ax + by)$ is bounded on $[0, T_{\max}[$ ; hence, $\lim_{t \to T_{\max}} y(t)$ exists. As a consequence, $y$ and $x = -(1/a)(\dot{y} + by)$ are bounded, and so is $\nabla \Phi(x)$ in view of (H-c). Then (c-DIN) shows that $\dot{x}$ is bounded too. Hence, $\lim_{t \to T_{\max}} x(t)$ exists. This classically yields a contradiction, and $T_{\max}$ must be equal to $+\infty$ . [The just-established limits $(x(T_{\max}^-),y(T_{\max}^-))$ furnish initial data for Cauchy--Lipschitz continuation, contradicting maximality.]

The last assertion, $(x,y)\in \mathcal{C}^1 (0, + \infty ;H)\times \mathcal{C}^2 (0, + \infty ;H)$ , immediately follows from (c-DIN).

(ii) Set $q(\lambda) = -(\lambda / \beta) |\dot{x}|^2 - b |\dot{y}|^2 + ((\lambda / \beta) - a) \langle \dot{x}, \dot{y} \rangle$ , $\lambda_{\min} = \beta (\sqrt{b} - \sqrt{b + a})^2$ , and $\lambda_{\max} = \beta (\sqrt{b} + \sqrt{b + a})^2$ . The inequality (30) yields:

$$
\dot {E} _ {\lambda_ {\min}} \leqslant q (\lambda_ {\min}) = - \left| \left(\sqrt {b} - \sqrt {b + a}\right) \dot {x} + \sqrt {b}   \dot {y} \right| ^ {2},
$$

$$
\dot {E} _ {\lambda_ {\max}} \leqslant q (\lambda_ {\max}) = - \left| \left(\sqrt {b} + \sqrt {b + a}\right) \dot {x} - \sqrt {b}   \dot {y} \right| ^ {2}.
$$

Since $q$ is an affine function of $\lambda$ for every $\lambda \in [\lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{\max}]$ , $E_{\lambda}$ lies between $q(\lambda_{\min})$ and $q(\lambda_{\max})$ and hence, is nonpositive. [More precisely, $\dot E_\lambda\leq q(\lambda)$ and affine interpolation of the two nonpositive endpoint values gives $q(\lambda)\leq0$; the phrase "$E_\lambda$" here refers to its derivative.] The energy $E_{\lambda}$ is then decreasing on $[0, +\infty[$ and converges since $\Phi$ is bounded from below on $C$ .

The inequality (32) shows that $\dot{x}$ and $\dot{y}$ belong to $L^{2}(0,+\infty;H)$ .

Now, considering two different values $\lambda, \lambda'$ in $[\lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{\max}]$ shows that $\Phi(x) = (1/(\lambda' - \lambda))(E_{\lambda'} - E_{\lambda})$ admits a limit as $t \to +\infty$ .

Hence, $|\dot{y}|^2 = |ax + by|^2 = 2(E_\lambda - \lambda \Phi(x))$ also admits a limit which necessarily is zero since $|\dot{y}|$ belongs to $L^2(0, +\infty; H)$ .

(iii) If $x$ is bounded, then $\nabla \Phi(x)$ is bounded (after $(\mathcal{H} - c)$ ), and $y = -(1/b)(ax + \dot{y})$ is bounded (recall $\dot{y} \to 0, t \to +\infty$ ). Further $\dot{x}$ is bounded in view of (c-DIN). Since $\dot{x}$ and $\dot{y}$ are bounded, $x$ and $y$ are Lipschitz continuous, which shows, in view of (c-DIN), that $\dot{x}$ itself is Lipschitz continuous. But $\dot{x}$ belongs to $L^2(0, +\infty; H)$ , hence, according to a classical argument, $\dot{x}(t) \to 0$ as $t \to +\infty$ .
items.remark: [Prove hint: projection variational inequality supplies (29); combine it with a quadratic energy]

items.name: Corollary 2.1
items.statement: Corollary 2.1. Assume that $\Phi: H \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies (H) and is coercive, i.e. $\lim_{|x| \to +\infty} \Phi(x) = +\infty$ . Then the solution $x$ of (DIN) is in $L^{\infty}(0, +\infty; H)$ . In particular, the properties in Theorem 2.1(iii) hold.
items.proof: Proof. It suffices to observe that (4) gives $(\alpha\beta+1)\Phi(x(t))\leqslant E(0)$ . This estimate and the coerciveness of $\Phi$ imply that the trajectory x remains bounded. [Indeed $\Phi(x(t))\leq E(0)/(\alpha\beta+1)$ for every $t$; the corresponding sublevel set is bounded by coercivity.] ☐
items.remark: [Prove hint: use the energy sublevel bound and coercivity]

items.name: Theorem 5.1
items.statement: Theorem 5.1. Let $\Phi$ be a convex function satisfying (H) and assume that $\operatorname{Argmin} \Phi \neq \emptyset$ . Let $x$ be a solution of (DIN). Then for all $z \in \operatorname{Argmin} \Phi$ , $\lim_{t \to +\infty} |x(t) - z|$ exists, and $x(t)$ weakly converges to a minimum point of $\Phi$ as $t \to +\infty$ .
items.proof:
Proof. Write $S = \operatorname{Argmin} \Phi$ and pick some $z$ in $S$ . In order to prove the existence of $\lim_{t \to +\infty} |x(t) - z|$ , we introduce an auxiliary energy:

$$
E _ {\varepsilon} (t) = E (t) + \varepsilon \left(\frac {\alpha}{2} \big | x (t) - z \big | ^ {2} + \big \langle \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big), x (t) - z \big \rangle\right), \tag {12}
$$

where $E$ is the energy defined by (2) and $\varepsilon$ is a positive parameter. Let us show that, by choosing $\varepsilon$ small enough, $E_{\varepsilon}$ is a Liapounov function for (DIN). Using (DIN) and (3), we have:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \dot {E} _ {\varepsilon} (t) = - (\alpha - \varepsilon) \big | \dot {x} (t) \big | ^ {2} - \beta \big | \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {2} \\ \left. - \varepsilon \big \langle \nabla \Phi (x (t)), x (t) - z \big \rangle + \varepsilon \big \langle \beta \nabla \Phi (x (t)), \dot {x} (t) \big \rangle . \right. \\ \end{array}
$$

Using the Young inequality for the last term, we obtain:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \dot {E} _ {\varepsilon} (t) \leqslant - \left(\alpha - \frac {3 \varepsilon}{2}\right) \big | \dot {x} (t) \big | ^ {2} - \beta \left(1 - \frac {\varepsilon \beta}{2}\right) \big | \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {2} \\ \left. - \varepsilon \big \langle \nabla \Phi (x (t)), x (t) - z \big \rangle . \right. \tag {13} \\ \end{array}
$$

Take $\varepsilon$ so small that each term in the previous expression is nonpositive [For instance take $0<\varepsilon<\min\{2\alpha/3,2/\beta\}$.  Convexity gives $\langle\nabla\Phi(x)-\nabla\Phi(z),x-z\rangle\geq0$ and $\nabla\Phi(z)=0$, hence the remaining inner-product term is nonpositive.] (for the last term, use the fact that $\nabla\Phi$ is monotone and $z\in S$ ); then $E_{\varepsilon}$ is nonincreasing and we readily obtain:

$$
\big \langle \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big), x (t) - z \big \rangle + \frac {\alpha}{2} \big | x (t) - z \big | ^ {2} \leqslant \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \big (E _ {\varepsilon} (0) - E (t) \big).
$$

Since $E(t)$ is bounded from below, because so is $\Phi$ , there exists some constant $M$ such that

$$
\left\langle \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big), x (t) - z \right\rangle + \frac {\alpha}{2} \big | x (t) - z \big | ^ {2} \leqslant M.
$$

As $\dot{x} + \beta \nabla \Phi(x)$ is bounded by Theorem 2.1(ii), $|x(t) - z|$ is bounded. Hence, $E_{\varepsilon}(t)$ , which is bounded from below and decreasing, admits a limit as $t \to +\infty$ . Moreover, Theorem 2.1(ii)-(iii) asserts the following: $\lim_{t \to +\infty} E(t)$ exists and $\lim_{t \to +\infty} \dot{x}(t) = \lim_{t \to +\infty} \nabla \Phi(x(t)) = 0$ ; hence, after (12), $\lim_{t \to +\infty} |x(t) - z|$ exists.

In order to apply the Opial lemma we need to prove that the weak cluster points of the trajectory x are in S. Let $\bar{x} \in H$ and $t_{n} \to +\infty$ be such that $x(t_{n}) \rightharpoonup \bar{x}$ . Using the convexity inequality, we have for any $z \in S$ ,

$$
\Phi (z) = \min \Phi \geqslant \Phi \big (x (t _ {n}) \big) + \big \langle \nabla \Phi \big (x (t _ {n}) \big), z - x (t _ {n}) \big \rangle .
$$

Since $\nabla\Phi(x(t_{n}))\to0$ and $\Phi$ is lower semicontinuous, we obtain:

$$
\min \Phi \geqslant \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to + \infty} \Phi \big (x (t _ {n}) \big) \geqslant \Phi (\bar {x}),
$$

which means that $\bar{x} \in S$ . [The displayed convexity inequality has an error term tending to $0$ because $x(t_n)$ is bounded and $\nabla\Phi(x(t_n))\to0$; weak lower semicontinuity of a continuous convex function gives the second inequality.] The Opial lemma then applies, ensuring the weak convergence of $x$ , and we also deduce that $\Phi(x(t)) \to \min \Phi$ as $t \to \infty$ .
items.remark: [Foundation: Hilbert.WeakConvergence] recall opial_lemma | [Prove hint: perturbed energy (12) gives Opial condition (b)]

items.name: Theorem 4.1
items.statement: Theorem 4.1. Let $x$ be a bounded solution of (DIN) and assume that $\Phi : \mathbb{R}^N \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is analytic. Then $\dot{x}$ belongs to $L^1(0, +\infty; H)$ and $x(t)$ converges towards a critical point of $\Phi$ as $t \to \infty$ .
items.proof:
Proof. Let $\omega(x)$ denote the $\omega$ -limit set of x. Classically ([19], e.g.), $\omega(x)$ is a compact connected set which consists of critical points of $\Phi$ . Moreover, from Theorem 2.1(ii), $\Phi$ assumes a constant value on $\omega(x)$ , which we may suppose to be 0. Further, $\text{dist}(x(t), \omega(x)) \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$ . [Here boundedness in $\mathbb R^N$ makes the orbit precompact; Theorem 2.1(iii) gives $\dot x(t),\nabla\Phi(x(t))\to0$, so the standard $\omega$-limit theorem yields the stated criticality.]

After Corollary 4.1, there exist some $T > 0$ and some $\theta \in ]0, 1/2[$ such that

$$
t \geqslant T \quad \Rightarrow \quad \left| \varPhi (x (t)) \right| ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant \left| \nabla \varPhi (x (t)) \right|. \tag {9}
$$

The proof of the convergence of x relies on the equality

$$
- \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} E (t) ^ {\theta} = - \dot {E} (t) E (t) ^ {\theta - 1}
$$

and on lower bounds for $-\dot{E}(t)$ and $E(t)^{\theta-1}$ involving $|\dot{x}(t)|$ ; recall that the energy E is defined by (2).

First, we have (recall (3)),

$$
- \dot {E} (t) \geqslant \frac {1}{2} \min (\alpha , \beta) \left\{\left| \dot {x} (t) \right| + \left| \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \right| \right\} ^ {2}. \tag {10}
$

Further, for $C = \max

[The lower bound (10) follows from $\alpha|\dot x|^2+\beta|\nabla\Phi|^2\geq\min(\alpha,\beta)(|\dot x|^2+|\nabla\Phi|^2)\geq\frac12\min(\alpha,\beta)(|\dot x|+|\nabla\Phi|)^2$.] (\alpha \beta +1,\beta^2)$ , we have (recall (2)),

$$
E (t) \leqslant C \big \{\left| \Phi (x (t)) \right| + \left| \dot {x} (t) \right| ^ {2} + \left| \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \right| ^ {2} \big \}.
$$

Hence (using the inequality $(r + s)^{1 - \theta}\leqslant r^{1 - \theta} + s^{1 - \theta})$

$$
E (t) ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant C ^ {1 - \theta} \big \{\big | \Phi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {1 - \theta} + \big | \dot {x} (t) \big | ^ {2 (1 - \theta)} + \big | \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {2 (1 - \theta)} \big \}.
$$

Using (9), we have for $t \geqslant T$ :

$$
E (t) ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant C ^ {1 - \theta} \big \{\big | \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) \big | + \big | \dot {x} (t) \big | ^ {2 (1 - \theta)} + \big | \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) \big | ^ {2 (1 - \theta)} \big \}.
$$

Since $|\nabla\Phi(x(t))|$ and $|\dot{x}(t)|$ tend to zero as $t \to \infty$ and since $2(1 - \theta) > 1$ , the quantities $|\nabla\Phi(x(t))|^{2(1-\theta)}$ and $|\dot{x}(t)|^{2(1-\theta)}$ are negligible with respect to $|\nabla\Phi(x(t))|$ and $|\dot{x}(t)|$ . Therefore, there is some constant D > 0 such that, for $t \geqslant T$ ,

$$
E (t) ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant D \Big \{\left| \nabla \varPhi (x (t)) \right| + \left| \dot {x} (t) \right| \Big \}. \tag {11}
$$

If $|\nabla\Phi(x(t))| + |\dot{x}(t)|$ happens to vanish at some time $t_{1} \geqslant T$ , then owing to the unicity of the solution to (DIN), $x(t)$ is equal to $x(t_{1})$ for $t \geqslant t_{1}$ , and the theorem is proved.

Else from (10) and (11) we obtain for $t \geqslant T$ :

$$
- \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} E (t) ^ {\theta} \geqslant \frac {1}{2 D} \min (\alpha , \beta) \big \{\left| \nabla \varPhi (x (t)) \right| + \left| \dot {x} (t) \right| \big \}.
$$

Since $\lim_{t\to\infty}E(t)$ exists, $|\dot{x}|$ belongs to $L^{1}([0,+\infty[)$ [Integrating the preceding differential inequality from $T$ to $R$ yields a bound by $E(T)^\theta-E(R)^\theta$; letting $R\to\infty$ proves integrability of $|\dot x|$ (and of $|\nabla\Phi(x)|$).] and consequently $\lim_{t\to\infty}x(t)$ exists. ☐
items.remark: [Prove hint: apply the uniform Lojasiewicz inequality on $\omega(x)$ to a fractional energy power]

items.name: Theorem 7.2
items.statement: Theorem 7.2. In addition to the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1, assume that $\Phi$ is convex and that $\operatorname{Argmin}_C\Phi$ , the set of minimizers of $\Phi$ on $C$ , is nonempty. Then for any solution $(x(t), y(t))$ of (c-DIN), $x(t)$ weakly converges to a minimizer of $\Phi$ on $C$ as $t$ goes to infinity.
items.proof:
Proof. First, let us establish some useful inequalities. Let $x^{*}$ be a minimizer of $\Phi$ on $C$ . Use the characteristic inequality for $P_{C}$ to write (it is implicit that the time variable $t$ varies in $[0, +\infty[$ in the following):

$$
\left\langle x ^ {*} - P _ {C} \big (x - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} \big), x - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} - P _ {C} \big (x - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} \big) \right\rangle \leqslant 0.
$$

In view of (c-DIN) we derive

$$
\left\langle x ^ {*} - x - \dot {x}, - \dot {x} - \beta \nabla \Phi (x) + \dot {y} \right\rangle \leqslant 0,
$$

$$
\langle x ^ {*} - x, \dot {y} - \dot {x} \rangle + \beta \big \langle \dot {x}, \nabla \Phi (x) \big \rangle \leqslant \big \langle x ^ {*} - x, \beta \nabla \Phi (x) \big \rangle - | \dot {x} | ^ {2}. \tag {33}
$$

But $\langle x^{*}-x,\nabla\Phi(x^{*})-\nabla\Phi(x)\rangle$ is nonnegative since $\Phi$ is convex; and $\langle x^{*}-x,-\nabla\Phi(x^{*})\rangle$ is nonnegative because $x^{*}$ is a minimizer of $\Phi$ on C. Hence, $\langle x^{*}-x,-\nabla\Phi(x)\rangle$ is nonnegative [Indeed add $\langle x^*-x,\nabla\Phi(x^*)-\nabla\Phi(x)\rangle\geq0$ and $\langle x^*-x,-\nabla\Phi(x^*)\rangle\geq0$ to obtain the claim.] and (33) entails

$$
\langle x ^ {*} - x, \dot {y} - \dot {x} \rangle + \beta \big \langle \dot {x}, \nabla \Phi (x) \big \rangle \leqslant - | \dot {x} | ^ {2}. \tag {34}
$$

Our aim now is to introduce an energy functional involving the term $|x^{*}-x|$ . Set

$$
F (t) = \bigl \langle x ^ {*} - x (t), a x (t) + b y (t) \bigr \rangle + \frac {1}{2} (b + a) \bigl | x ^ {*} - x (t) \bigr | ^ {2} + b \beta \varPhi \bigl (x (t) \bigr).
$$

We have

$$
\dot {F} = b \big (\langle x ^ {*} - x, \dot {y} - \dot {x} \rangle + \big \langle \dot {x}, \beta \nabla \varPhi (x) \big \rangle \big) + \langle \dot {x}, \dot {y} \rangle ,
$$

and in view of (34) we obtain:

$$
\dot {F} \leqslant \langle \dot {x}, \dot {y} \rangle - b | \dot {x} | ^ {2} \leqslant - \left(b - \frac {3}{2}\right) | \dot {x} | ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} | \dot {y} - \dot {x} | ^ {2}. \tag {35}
$$

In view of (31) and (35) we may fix some $\varepsilon > 0$ so small that the function $\mathcal{E}:\mathbb{R}\mapsto H$ defined by:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {E} = E _ {a + 2 b} + \varepsilon F = (a + 2 b + \varepsilon b \beta) \varPhi (x) + \frac {1}{2} | a x + b y | ^ {2} \\ + \varepsilon \langle x ^ {*} - x, a x + b y \rangle + \frac {\varepsilon}{2} (a + b) | x ^ {*} - x | ^ {2} \\ \end{array}
$$

is decreasing and, hence, bounded above. [Combining (31) and (35), choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that each positive contribution from $\varepsilon\dot F$ is dominated by the strictly negative dissipation terms in $\dot E_{\beta(a+2b)}$.] Since $\Phi(x)$ is bounded from below on C, the quantity

$$
- | a x + b y | | x ^ {*} - x | + \frac {1}{2} (b + a) | x - x ^ {*} | ^ {2},
$$

which is less than $\langle x^{*}-x, ax+by\rangle+(1/2)(b+a)|x^{*}-x|^{2}$ , is bounded from above; hence, $|x^{*}-x|$ is bounded because $\dot{y}=ax+by$ is bounded (Theorem (7.1)(ii)). From that we deduce that E is bounded below and admits a limit as $t\to+\infty$ . Now in the expression of E the first three terms are known to have a limit, as $t\to+\infty$ , hence, $|x^{*}-x|$ has a limit.

In order to apply Opial's lemma, we now show that any weak limit point $x_{\infty}$ of $x$ belongs to $\mathrm{Argmin}_C\Phi$ . Let $x^{*}$ be an element of $\mathrm{Argmin}_C\Phi$ . Invoking the convexity of $\Phi$ and inequality (33), we have:

$$
\Phi (x ^ {*}) \geqslant \Phi (x (t)) + \big \langle x ^ {*} - x, \nabla \Phi (x) \big \rangle ,
$$

$$
\varPhi (x ^ {*}) \geqslant \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) + \frac {1}{\beta} \langle x ^ {*} - x, \dot {y} - \dot {x} \rangle + \frac {1}{\beta} \big \langle \dot {x}, \dot {x} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x) \big \rangle .
$$

Since $|\dot{x}| + |\dot{y}| \to 0$ as $t \to +\infty$ , and since $(x^{*} - x)$ and $(\dot{x} + \beta \nabla \Phi(x))$ are bounded, we have:

$$
\langle x ^ {*} - x, \dot {y} - \dot {x} \rangle + \left\langle \dot {x}, \dot {x} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x) \right\rangle\rightarrow 0, \quad t \rightarrow + \infty .
$$

So, if $t_{n}$ is a sequence going to infinity such that $x(t_{n})$ weakly converges to $x_{\infty}$ , we have $\Phi(x^{*}) \geqslant \liminf\Phi(x(t_{n})) \geqslant \Phi(x_{\infty})$ . Hence, $x_{\infty}$ is a minimizer of $\Phi$ on C [Since $x(t_n)\in C$ and $C$ is closed convex, it is weakly closed, hence $x_\infty\in C$; the last inequality therefore identifies it as a constrained minimizer.], and Opial's lemma entails that $x(t)$ weakly converges to $x_{\infty}$ . ☐
items.remark: [Foundation: Hilbert.WeakConvergence] recall opial_lemma | [Prove hint: establish distance limits through $\mathcal E$, then verify weak cluster points]

items.name: Proposition 5.1
items.statement: Proposition 5.1. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, if, moreover, $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Argmin}\Phi) \neq \emptyset$ then every trajectory of (DIN) converges to a minimizer of $\Phi$ with respect to the strong topology of $H$ .
items.proof:
Proof. Fix $z \in \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Argmin}\Phi)$ so that there exists $\rho > 0$ such that for every $z' \in H$ with $|z' - z| < \rho$ then $z' \in \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Argmin}\Phi)$ and consequently $\nabla\Phi(z') = 0$ . By monotonicity of $\nabla\Phi$ , we have:

$$
\left\langle \nabla \varPhi (y), y - z \right\rangle \geqslant \left\langle \nabla \varPhi (y), z ^ {\prime} - z \right\rangle
$$

for all $y \in H$ and $z' \in H$ with $\nabla \Phi(z') = 0$ . Thus, for every $y \in H$ ,

$ [Choose $z'=z-\\rho\\nabla\\Phi(y)/|\\nabla\\Phi(y)|$ when $\\nabla\\Phi(y)\\ne0$ (and argue trivially otherwise); this point lies in the interior minimizer ball, and substitution gives the asserted lower bound.]
\big \langle \nabla \varPhi (y), y - z \big \rangle \geqslant \rho \big | \nabla \varPhi (y) \big |.
$$

Specialize y to $x(t)$ to obtain for all $t \geqslant 0$ and all $z \in \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Argmin}\Phi)$ :

$$
\left\langle \nabla \Phi (x (t)), x (t) - z \right\rangle \geqslant \rho \left| \nabla \Phi (x (t)) \right|. \tag {14}
$$

Now, for $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough, the inequality (13) may be simplified to

$$
0 \leqslant \varepsilon \big \langle \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), x (t) - z \big \rangle \leqslant - \dot {E} _ {\varepsilon} (t);
$$

integrating the latter yields

$$
0 \leqslant \varepsilon \int_ {0} ^ {t} \big \langle \nabla \varPhi (x (s)), x (s) - z \big \rangle \mathrm{d} s \leqslant E _ {\varepsilon} (0) - E _ {\varepsilon} (t).
$$

Since $\lim_{t\to +\infty}E_{\varepsilon}(t)$ exists, after the proof of Theorem 5.1, we deduce that $\langle \nabla \Phi (x),x - z\rangle$ belongs to $L^1 (0, + \infty)$ , and so does $|\nabla \Phi (x)|$ in view of (14). If we now integrate (DIN),

$$
\dot {x} (t) + \alpha x (t) + \beta \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \nabla \varPhi \big (x (s) \big) \mathrm{d} s = \dot {x} _ {0} + \alpha x _ {0} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x _ {0}),
$$

we see that $\lim_{t\to +\infty}x(t)$ exists in $H$ [The integral of $\nabla\Phi(x(s))$ converges because it is in $L^1$, while the two remaining terms on the left have limits; solve the identity for $x(t)$.] , since $\lim_{t\to +\infty}\dot{x} (t) = \lim_{t\to +\infty}\nabla \varPhi (x(t)) = 0$ , after Theorem 2.1(iii).
items.remark: [Prove hint: an interior minimizer ball converts monotonicity into an $L^1$ bound for the gradient]

items.name: Proposition 5.2
items.statement: Proposition 5.2. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, if, moreover, $\Phi$ is supposed to be even, i.e. $\forall y\in H,\Phi (y) = \Phi (-y)$ , then every trajectory of (DIN) converges to a minimizer of $\Phi$ with respect to the strong topology of $H$ .
items.proof:
Proof. Let us successively consider the case $\alpha \beta \leqslant 1$ and the case $\alpha \beta > 1$ .

1. Case $\alpha \beta \leqslant 1$ . Fix $t_0 > 0$ and define $g_{t_0}:[0,t_0]\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ by

$$
g _ {t _ {0}} (t) = \left| x (t) \right| ^ {2} - \left| x (t _ {0}) \right| ^ {2} - \frac {1}{2} \big | x (t) - x (t _ {0}) \big | ^ {2}.
$$

We have $\dot{g}_{t_{0}}(t)=\langle\dot{x}(t),x(t)+x(t_{0})\rangle$ and $\ddot{g}_{t_{0}}(t)=\langle\ddot{x}(t),x(t)+x(t_{0})\rangle+|\dot{x}(t)|^{2}$ . From this we obtain:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \ddot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (t) + \alpha \dot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (t) = \left\langle - \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi (x (t)) \dot {x} (t) - \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), x (t) + x (t _ {0}) \right\rangle + \left| \dot {x} (t) \right| ^ {2} \\ = \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \bigl \langle - \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), x (t) + x (t _ {0}) \bigr \rangle + \bigl \langle \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), \dot {x} (t) \bigr \rangle \\ + \frac {1}{\beta} \bigl \langle - \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), x (t) + x (t _ {0}) \bigr \rangle + \left| \dot {x} (t) \right| ^ {2} \\ = \mathrm{e} ^ {- (1 / \beta) t} \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \mathrm{e} ^ {(1 / \beta) t} \bigl \langle - \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), x (t) + x (t _ {0}) \bigr \rangle \\ + \left\langle \dot {x} (t) + \beta \nabla \Phi (x (t)), \dot {x} (t) \right\rangle . \\ \end{array}
$$

Set $f(t) = \langle \dot{x}(t) + \beta \nabla \Phi(x(t)), \dot{x}(t) \rangle$ . Since $\dot{x}$ and $\nabla \Phi(x)$ are in $L^2(0, +\infty; H)$ , $f$ belongs to $L^1(0, +\infty)$ . We have:

$$
\frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \big [ \mathrm{e} ^ {\alpha t} \dot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (t) \big ] = \mathrm{e} ^ {(\alpha - 1 / \beta) t} \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \mathrm{e} ^ {(1 / \beta) t} \big \langle - \beta \nabla \varPhi (x (t)), x (t) + x (t _ {0}) \big \rangle + \mathrm{e} ^ {\alpha t} f (t)
$$

and so, for every $t \in ]0, t_0]$ ,

$$
\mathrm{e} ^ {\alpha t} \dot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (t) - \dot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (0) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {(\alpha - 1 / \beta) \tau} \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s} \big [ \beta \mathrm{e} ^ {s / \beta} \omega_ {t _ {0}} (s) \big ] _ {s = \tau} \mathrm{d} \tau + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {\alpha \tau} f (\tau) \mathrm{d} \tau ,
$$

with $\omega_{t_0}(s) = \langle -\nabla \Phi (x(s)), x(s) + x(t_0)\rangle$ . An integration by parts yields

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {(\alpha - 1 / \beta) \tau} \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s} \big [ \beta \mathrm{e} ^ {s / \beta} \omega_ {t _ {0}} (s) \big ] _ {s = \tau} \mathrm{d} \tau \\ = \beta \mathrm{e} ^ {\alpha t} \omega_ {t _ {0}} (t) - \beta \omega_ {t _ {0}} (0) + (1 - \alpha \beta) \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {\alpha \tau} \omega_ {t _ {0}} (\tau) \mathrm{d} \tau . \\ \end{array}
$$

We conclude that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \dot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (t) = \big \langle \dot {x} _ {0} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x _ {0}), x _ {0} + x (t _ {0}) \big \rangle \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t} + \beta \omega_ {t _ {0}} (t) \\ + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha (t - \tau)} \big [ (1 - \alpha \beta) \omega_ {t _ {0}} (\tau) + f (\tau) \big ] \mathrm{d} \tau . \\ \end{array}
$$

Set $F(t) = (1/2)|\dot{x}(t)|^2 + \Phi(x(t))$ , which is nonincreasing because $\Phi$ is convex (in fact, $\dot{F}(t) = -\alpha|\dot{x}(t)|^2 - \beta\langle\nabla^2\Phi(x(t))\dot{x}(t), \dot{x}(t)\rangle \leqslant 0$ ). Then, for all $t \in [0, t_0]$ ,

$$
F (t) \geqslant F (t _ {0}) = \frac {1}{2} \big | \dot {x} (t _ {0}) \big | ^ {2} + \varPhi \big (x (t _ {0}) \big) = \frac {1}{2} \big | \dot {x} (t _ {0}) \big | ^ {2} + \varPhi \big (- x (t _ {0}) \big).
$$

By convexity of $\Phi$ ,

$$
\Phi \big (- x (t _ {0}) \big) \geqslant \Phi \big (x (t) \big) + \big \langle \nabla \Phi \big (x (t) \big), - x (t _ {0}) - x (t) \big \rangle
$$

and, consequently,

$$
\omega_ {t _ {0}} (t) = \left\langle - \nabla \varPhi \big (x (t) \big), x (t) + x (t _ {0}) \right\rangle \leqslant \frac {1}{2} \Big | \dot {x} (t) \Big | ^ {2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dot {g} _ {t _ {0}} (t) \leqslant \left\langle \dot {x} _ {0} + \beta \nabla \Phi (x _ {0}), x _ {0} + x (t _ {0}) \right\rangle \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t} + \frac {\beta}{2} \big | \dot {x} (t) \big | ^ {2} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha (t - \tau)} h (\tau) \mathrm{d} \tau ,
$$

where $h(t) = ((1 - \alpha \beta) / 2)|\dot{x}(t)|^2 + |f(t)| \in L^1(0, \infty)$ . Hence, for all $t \in [0, t_0]$ ,

$$
\begin{array}{l} g _ {t _ {0}} (t _ {0}) - g _ {t _ {0}} (t) \leqslant \frac {1}{\alpha} \big \langle \dot {x} _ {0} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x _ {0}), x _ {0} + x (t _ {0}) \big \rangle \big (\mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t} - \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t _ {0}} \big) \\ + \frac {\beta}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {t _ {0}} \left| \dot {x} (\tau) \right| ^ {2} \mathrm{d} \tau + \int_ {t} ^ {t _ {0}} \int_ {0} ^ {\theta} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha (\theta - \tau)} h (\tau) \mathrm{d} \tau \mathrm{d} \theta \\ \end{array}
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{2} \big | x (t _ {0}) - x (t) \big | ^ {2} \leqslant \big | x (t) \big | ^ {2} - \big | x (t _ {0}) \big | ^ {2} \\ + \frac {1}{\alpha} \bigl \langle \dot {x} _ {0} + \beta \nabla \varPhi (x _ {0}), x _ {0} + x (t _ {0}) \bigr \rangle \bigl (\mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t} - \mathrm{e} ^ {- \alpha t _ {0}} \bigr) + \int_ {t} ^ {t _ {0}} p (\theta) \mathrm{d} \theta , \\ \end{array}
$$

where $p \in L^{1}(0, \infty)$ . We know that $x(t) \rightharpoonup x_{\infty}$ as $t \to \infty$ where $x_{\infty} \in \operatorname{Argmin} \Phi$ . Moreover, for all $z \in \operatorname{Argmin} \Phi$ there exists some $l_{z} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|x(t) - z|^{2} \to l_{z}$ , as $t \to \infty$ (see Theorem 5.1). Since $\Phi$ is even, 0 is a minimizer of $\Phi$ so that there is some $l_{0} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\lim_{t \to \infty} |x(t)|^{2} = l_{0}$ . From the inequality above it follows that $\{x(t): t \to \infty\}$ is a Cauchy net in $H$ [Let first $t$, then $t_0$, tend to infinity.  The norm-difference term, the exponentially decaying term, and the $L^1$ tail all tend to $0$, so the displayed estimate forces $|x(t_0)-x(t)|\to0$ uniformly for large $t,t_0$.] , hence, $x(t) \to x_{\infty}$ strongly in $H$ .

2. Case $\alpha\beta > 1$ . The conclusion follows in this case from a well-known result of Bruck [16] [Under Proposition 6.1 the equivalent energy on $H\times H$ is convex and even when $\Phi$ is convex and even, so the cited gradient-flow theorem applies; projecting the strongly convergent pair gives strong convergence of $x$.] applied to an equivalent gradient-type first-order system defined on $H \times H$ (see Section 6.3). ☐
items.remark: [Prove hint: the $\alpha\beta>1$ branch requires ext_thm_3 after the gradient-system equivalence]

items.name: Quadratic potential remark
items.statement:
Remark. If $\Phi(x) = (1/2)\langle Ax, x\rangle$ where $A: H \mapsto H$ is a positive self-adjoint and bounded linear operator, then $\operatorname{Argmin} \Phi = \operatorname{Ker} A = \{z \in H: Az = 0\}$ and $x(t)$ strongly converges in $H$ to the projection of $x_0 + (1/\alpha)\dot{x}_0$ on $\operatorname{Ker} A$ . Indeed, for every $z \in \operatorname{Ker} A$ and $t > 0$ , we have:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \big \langle \dot {x} (t) + \alpha x (t) - \dot {x} _ {0} - \alpha x _ {0}, z \big \rangle = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \big \langle - \beta \nabla^ {2} \varPhi \big (x (\tau) \big) \dot {x} (\tau) - \nabla \varPhi \big (x (\tau) \big), z \big \rangle \mathrm{d} \tau \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left\langle - \beta A \dot {x} (\tau) - A x (\tau), z \right\rangle \mathrm{d} \tau \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left\langle - \beta \dot {x} (\tau) - x (\tau), A z \right\rangle \mathrm{d} \tau = 0. \\ \end{array}
$$

Since $\dot{x}(t) \to 0$ and $x(t) \to x_{\infty} \in \operatorname{Ker} A$ strongly, we deduce that $\langle x_{\infty} - x_0 - (1/\alpha)\dot{x}_0, z \rangle = 0$ for all $z \in \operatorname{Ker} A$ , which proves our claim.
items.remark: [Foundation: Projection.BestApproximation] recall isChebyshev_of_nonempty_isClosed_convex

external_theorems.name: Opial's Lemma
external_theorems.statement:
Lemma 5.1 (Opial). Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $x:[0, +\infty [\mapsto H$ a function such that there exists a nonempty set $S \subseteq H$ verifying:

(a) if $x(t_n) \rightharpoonup \bar{x}$ weakly in $H$ for some $t_n \to +\infty$ then $\bar{x} \in S$ ;  
(b) $\forall z\in S,\lim_{t\to +\infty}|x(t) - z|$ exists.

Then, $x(t)$ weakly converges as $t \to +\infty$ to an element of $S$ .
external_theorems.proof: Cited from: Z. Opial, Weak convergence of the sequence of successive approximations for nonexpansive mappings, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 73 (1967) 591–597.
external_theorems.source: Z. Opial, Weak convergence of the sequence of successive approximations for nonexpansive mappings, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 73 (1967) 591–597.

external_theorems.name: Cauchy--Lipschitz continuation theorem
external_theorems.statement: Let $X$ be a Banach space and $F:X\\to X$ be locally Lipschitz. For every $Y_0\\in X$, the equation $\\dot Y=F(Y)$ has a unique maximal classical solution. If its maximal time $T_{\\max}$ is finite and $Y(t)$ has a finite limit as $t\\uparrow T_{\\max}$, then the solution extends past $T_{\\max}$.
external_theorems.proof: Cited from: standard Cauchy--Lipschitz/Picard--Lindel"of theorem for Banach-space ODEs.
external_theorems.remark: [Prove hint: show the phase-space vector field is locally Lipschitz, then use the continuation clause]

external_theorems.name: Bruck strong-convergence theorem for even convex gradient flows
external_theorems.statement: If $\\mathcal E$ is an even convex differentiable functional on a Hilbert space with nonempty minimizer set, then the trajectory of its gradient flow $\\dot X+\\nabla\\mathcal E(X)=0$ converges strongly to a minimizer under the hypotheses used in Proposition 5.2.
external_theorems.proof: Cited from: R. E. Bruck, Asymptotic convergence of nonlinear contraction semigroups in Hilbert space, J. Funct. Anal. 18 (1975), 15--26.
external_theorems.source: R. E. Bruck, Asymptotic convergence of nonlinear contraction semigroups in Hilbert space, J. Funct. Anal. 18 (1975), 15--26.

external_theorems.name: Lojasiewicz Lemma
external_theorems.statement:
Lemma 4.1 (Lojasiewicz). Let $\Phi : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function which is supposed to be analytic in a neighbourhood of a critical point $a$ . Then, there exist $\sigma > 0$ and $\theta \in ]0, 1/2[$ such that $^2$

$$
| x - a | <   \sigma \quad \Rightarrow \quad \left| \Phi (x) - \Phi (a) \right| ^ {1 - \theta} \leqslant \left| \nabla \Phi (x) \right|.
$$
external_theorems.proof: Cited from: S. Lojasiewicz, Ensembles semi-analytiques, IHES Notes (1965).
external_theorems.source: S. Lojasiewicz, Ensembles semi-analytiques, IHES Notes (1965).
external_theorems.remark: [Note: the paper needs the local gradient inequality near a critical point]

external_theorems.name: Properties of the $omega$-limit set of a bounded finite-dimensional trajectory
external_theorems.statement: For a bounded trajectory of a continuous autonomous flow in $\\mathbb{R}^N$, $\\omega(x)$ is nonempty, compact, and connected, and $\\operatorname{dist}(x(t),\\omega(x))\\to0$. If along the trajectory the velocity and the gradient of a $C^1$ Lyapunov potential tend to $0$, then every point of $\\omega(x)$ is a critical point of that potential.
external_theorems.proof: Cited from: A. Haraux, Systèmes Dynamiques Dissipatifs et Applications, RMA 17, Masson, 1991, as cited in the proof of Theorem 4.1.
external_theorems.source: A. Haraux, Systèmes Dynamiques Dissipatifs et Applications, RMA 17, Masson, 1991.
external_theorems.remark: [Note: the stated compactness uses the finite-dimensional hypothesis $H=mathbb{R}^N$]
